sources.title: Intestinal microbiota metabolism of L-carnitine, a nutrient in red meat, promotes atherosclerosis

quotes: Omnivorous subjects are shown to produce significantly more TMAO than vegans/vegetarians following ingestion of L-carnitine through a microbiota-dependent mechanism.

Chronic dietary L-carnitine supplementation in mice significantly altered cecal microbial composition, markedly enhanced synthesis of TMA/TMAO, and increased atherosclerosis, but not following suppression of intestinal microbiota.
Aortic root atherosclerotic plaque quantification revealed approximately a doubling in disease burden compared to normal chow fed animals

Plasma L-carnitine levels in subjects undergoing cardiac evaluation ( _n_ = 2,595) predict increased risks for both prevalent cardiovascular disease (CVD) and incident major adverse cardiac events (MI, stroke or death), but only among subjects with concurrently high TMAO levels.
sources.notes: Landmark L-carnitine challenge study: omnivores vs vegans/vegetarians; microbiota dependence via antibiotics; mice supplementation atherosclerosis; plasma carnitine predicts MACE only with high TMAO (n=2,595). PMC full text; PubMed abstract at PMID 23563705.

sources.title: Fish protein increases circulating levels of trimethylamine-N-oxide and accelerates aortic lesion formation in apoE null mice
sources.authors: Yazdekhasti N; Brandsch C; Schmidt N; Schloesser A; Huebbe P; Rimbach G; Stangl GI
quotes: Fish protein intake was accompanied by increased serum concentrations of trimethylamine-N-oxide (7.03 ± 2.83 μmol/L), as compared with casein (0.92 ± 0.46 μmol/L) and soy protein (1.32 ± 0.54 μmol/L) intake.
Morphometric analysis of the aorta revealed that the atherosclerotic plaque area of fish protein fed mice was twofold larger than that in casein- or soy protein-fed mice.
sources.notes: ApoE-null mice: 16-week fish-protein Western diet raised serum TMAO ~7 uM (vs ~1 uM casein/soy) and doubled aortic plaque area - the animal-side counterpart of the fish paradox. sources.title: Revisiting the Role of Carnitine in Heart Disease Through the Lens of the Gut Microbiota
sources.authors: Demarquoy J
quotes: Dietary interventions, such as increasing fiber, polyphenols, and probiotics, can modulate the gut microbiota to reduce TMAO production.
sources.notes: 2024 review balancing carnitine's roles against the TMAO concern; fiber, polyphenols and probiotics as microbiota-modulating levers to reduce TMAO production. claims.claim: In the founding 2011 Nature study, dietary supplementation of mice with choline, TMAO or betaine promoted up-regulation of multiple macrophage scavenger receptors linked to atherosclerosis, and supplementation with choline or TMAO promoted atherosclerosis itself.
claims.quote: Dietary supplementation of mice with choline, TMAO or betaine promoted up-regulation of multiple macrophage scavenger receptors linked to atherosclerosis, and supplementation with choline or TMAO promoted atherosclerosis.

claims.claim: Omnivorous human subjects produced significantly more TMAO than vegans or vegetarians following ingestion of L-carnitine, through a microbiota-dependent mechanism.
claims.quote: Omnivorous subjects are shown to produce significantly more TMAO than vegans/vegetarians following ingestion of L-carnitine through a microbiota-dependent mechanism.

claims.claim: Chronic dietary L-carnitine supplementation in mice altered cecal microbial composition, markedly enhanced TMA/TMAO synthesis and increased atherosclerosis, but none of this occurred when the intestinal microbiota was concurrently suppressed.
claims.quote: Chronic dietary L-carnitine supplementation in mice significantly altered cecal microbial composition, markedly enhanced synthesis of TMA/TMAO, and increased atherosclerosis, but not following suppression of intestinal microbiota.

claims.claim: In the host step of the pathway, hepatic flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 converts gut-microbiota-derived trimethylamine to TMAO, which is then excreted in urine.
claims.quote: FMO3 converts the odorous TMA to nonodorous TMA N-oxide (TMAO), which is excreted in urine.

claims.claim: Following oral deuterium-labeled L-carnitine ingestion, omnivores showed a more than 20-fold greater generation of labelled TMAO than vegans/vegetarians, although fasting endogenous plasma L-carnitine and gamma-butyrobetaine levels were similar between diet groups.
claims.quote: Moreover, a striking increase in d3-TMAO generation was observed in omnivores over vegans/vegetarians (>20-fold; _P_ = 0.001) following oral d3-l-carnitine ingestion, whereas fasting endogenous plasma l-carnitine and γBB levels were similar in vegans/vegetarians ( _n_ = 32) versus omnivores ( _n_ = 40).

claims.claim: A systematic review of 11 trials found that prolonged oral L-carnitine supplementation (1-4 g/day for 12 or 24 weeks) in healthy subjects induces an increase of fasting plasma TMAO that was not associated with changes in inflammatory or oxidative-stress markers.
claims.quote: LC supplementation was also noted to induce an increase of fasting plasma trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) levels, which was not associated with modification of determined inflammatory nor oxidative stress markers.

claims.claim: Serum TMAO is markedly higher in dialysis-dependent CKD patients than in healthy controls (median 94.4 uM vs 3.3 uM), and renal transplantation substantially reduces TMAO concentrations.
claims.quote: TMAO concentrations were markedly higher in patients receiving dialysis (median \[interquartile range\], 94.4 μM \[54.8-133.0 μM\] for dialysis-dependent patients versus 3.3 μM \[3.1-6.0 μM\] for healthy controls; P<0.001); whereas renal transplantation resulted in substantial reductions in TMAO concentrations (median \[min-max\] 71.2 μM \[29.2-189.7 μM\] pretransplant versus 11.4 μM \[8.9-20.2 μM\] post-transplant; P=0.03).

claims.claim: Among 521 stable CKD subjects, top-quartile plasma TMAO was associated with a 2.8-fold increased 5-year mortality risk, which remained significant after adjustment for traditional risk factors, hsCRP and eGFR (hazard ratio 1.93).
claims.quote: Within CKD subjects, higher (4th vs. 1st quartile) plasma TMAO level was associated with a 2.8-fold increased mortality risk. Following adjustments for traditional risk factors, hsCRP and eGFR, elevated TMAO levels remained predictive of 5-year mortality risk (HR 1.93 \[95%CI 1.13–3.29\], p<0.05).

claims.claim: In animal models, chronically elevated dietary choline or TMAO directly led to progressive renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis and dysfunction.
claims.quote: In animal models, elevated dietary choline or TMAO directly led to progressive renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis and dysfunction.

claims.claim: In 10,564 community-based US adults, higher serial plasma TMAO was associated with higher incident-CKD risk (hazard ratios up to 2.24 across quintiles) and greater annualized eGFR decline, with monotonic dose-response relationships.
claims.quote: Higher TMAO levels were associated with higher risk of incident CKD (second to fifth versus first quintile hazard ratio \[95% confidence interval\]=1.65 \[1.22 to 2.23\], 1.68 \[1.26 to 2.25\], 2.28 \[1.72 to 3.02\], and 2.24 \[1.68 to 2.98\], respectively) and greater annualized eGFR decline (second to fifth versus first quintile annualized eGFR change=−0.21 \[−0.32 to −0.09\], −0.17 \[−0.29 to −0.05\], −0.35 \[−0.47 to −0.22\], and −0.43 \[−0.56 to −0.30\] ml/min per 1.73 m2, respectively) with monotonic dose–response relationships.

claims.claim: In a post hoc analysis of the EVOLVE trial (n=1243 maintenance hemodialysis patients), baseline serum TMAO showed no association with the composite cardiovascular outcome or all-cause mortality.
claims.quote: We found no evidence linking TMAO to adverse clinical outcomes in patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis with moderate to severe secondary hyperparathyroidism.

claims.claim: In 4,007 patients undergoing elective coronary angiography, increased fasting plasma TMAO was associated with an increased risk of incident major adverse cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 2.54 for highest vs lowest quartile).
claims.quote: Increased plasma levels of TMAO were associated with an increased risk of a major adverse cardiovascular event (hazard ratio for highest vs. lowest TMAO quartile, 2.54; 95% confidence interval, 1.96 to 3.28; P<0.001).

claims.claim: A dose-response meta-analysis of 17 clinical studies found high plasma TMAO associated with all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.91) and major adverse cardio/cerebrovascular events (hazard ratio 1.67), with mortality risk increasing 7.6% per 10 umol/L of TMAO.
claims.quote: High TMAO plasma levels were associated with increased incidence of all-cause mortality \[14 studies for 16 cohorts enrolling 15 662 subjects, hazard ratio (HR): 1.91; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.40-2.61, P < 0.0001, I2 = 94%\] and MACCE (5 studies for 6 cohorts enrolling 13 944 subjects, HR: 1.67, 95% CI: 1.33-2.11, P < 0.00001, I2 = 46%,). Dose-response meta-analysis revealed that the relative risk (RR) for all-cause mortality increased by 7.6% per each 10 μmol/L increment of TMAO \[summary RR: 1.07, 95% CI (1.04-1.11), P < 0.0001; based on seven studies\].

claims.claim: In the community-based MESA cohort (6,767 adults free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at baseline), plasma TMAO was associated with incident ASCVD in a dose-dependent fashion (top-quintile hazard ratio 1.33) over a median 11.3-year follow-up.
claims.quote: After multivariate adjustment, TMAO associated with higher risk of ASCVD in a dose-dependent fashion, with hazard ratios across quintiles of 1.02, 1.17, 1.23, and 1.33 (95% CI 1.02, 1.74), respectively, compared to the lowest quintile (P-trend = 0.01).

claims.claim: In bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses, genetically predicted higher TMAO and carnitine were not associated with cardiometabolic outcomes, and the authors conclude that observational TMAO-cardiovascular evidence may be due to confounding or reverse causality.
claims.quote: Our Mendelian randomization findings support that T2DM and kidney disease increase TMAO levels and that observational evidence for cardiovascular diseases may be due to confounding or reverse causality.

claims.claim: In ApoE-/- mice expressing human CETP and chronically fed high-dose L-carnitine, plasma TMAO levels inversely correlated with aortic lesion size, and high TMAO significantly correlated with smaller aortic lesion area.
claims.quote: Surprisingly, and independently from treatment group, TMAO levels inversely correlated with aortic lesion size in both aortic root and thoracic aorta. High TMAO levels were found to significantly correlate with smaller aortic lesion area. Plasma lipid and lipoprotein levels did not change with treatment nor with TMAO levels, suggesting that the observed effects on lesion area were independent from lipid changes. **Conclusion:** These findings suggest that TMAO slows aortic lesion formation in this mouse model and may have a protective effect against atherosclerosis development in humans.

claims.claim: In a 6-month randomized placebo-controlled trial of 2 g/day L-carnitine in metabolic syndrome (n=157), carotid total plaque volume did not differ between arms, but the L-carnitine group showed a 9.3% greater increase in carotid atherosclerotic stenosis.
claims.quote: In 157 participants (L-C N = 76, placebo N = 81), no difference in TPV change between arms was found. The L-C group had a greater increase in carotid atherosclerotic stenosis of 9.3% (p = 0.02) than the placebo group.

claims.claim: In healthy sedentary and endurance-trained males, neither a 4-hour high-fat challenge meal nor a subsequent 5-day high-fat diet evoked a detectable change in plasma TMAO, and fasting and postprandial TMAO did not differ between training groups.
claims.quote: Neither the HFC nor the HFD evoked a detectable change in plasma TMAO ( _p_ > 0.05) in either group.

claims.claim: Consumption of fish meals (fish sticks, cod and, to a lesser extent, salmon) led to significant increases in circulating TMAO that returned to baseline within one day in all participants with normal renal function.
claims.quote: Consumption of fish sticks, cod, and to lesser extent, salmon, lead to significant increases in circulating TMAO levels. Within one day, circulating TMAO concentrations in all participants returned to baseline levels.

claims.claim: In two randomized controlled trials, diets naturally rich in marine omega-3 fatty acids or whole-grain cereals significantly increased plasma TMAO, leading the authors to conclude TMAO is not a universally valid biomarker of cardiometabolic risk independent of background diet.
claims.quote: Diets rich in LCn3 of marine origin or WGCs significantly increased plasma TMAO concentration. These changes mirrored the direct associations between TMAO concentrations and intakes of fish and WGCs, suggesting that TMAO reflects intakes of these healthy foods and, therefore, it is not a universally valid biomarker of cardiometabolic risk independent of the background diet.

claims.claim: The renal risks and benefits of L-carnitine in athletes and bodybuilders have not been evaluated in the literature, although L-carnitine up to 6,000 mg/day is generally considered a safe supplement in healthy adults.
claims.quote: The risks and benefits of L-carnitine on the athletes' and bodybuilders' kidney have not been evaluated yet. However, L-carnitine up to 6000 mg/day is generally considered to be a safe supplement at least in healthy adults.

claims.claim: Across human studies, TMAO levels do not consistently correlate with aerobic fitness, habitual physical activity or training status, and exercise-only interventions rarely produce significant changes in circulating TMAO while dietary manipulation exerts substantially stronger effects.
claims.quote: Across human studies, TMAO levels do not consistently correlate with aerobic fitness, habitual physical activity, or training status. Exercise-only interventions rarely produce significant changes in circulating TMAO concentrations, whereas dietary manipulation and precursor supplementation exert substantially stronger effects.

claims.claim: A formal risk assessment identified 2,000 mg/day of L-carnitine equivalents as the observed safe level for chronic supplementation, while noting that data for intakes above this level are not sufficient for a confident conclusion of long-term safety.
claims.quote: The OSL risk assessment method indicates that the evidence of safety is strong at intakes up to 2000mg/day l-carnitine equivalents for chronic supplementation, and this level is identified as the OSL.

claims.claim: Several animal studies reported neutral or even beneficial effects of TMAO or its precursors in cardiovascular disease models, supporting the clinically proven beneficial effects of L-carnitine or a seafood-rich diet (naturally containing TMAO) on cardiometabolic health.
claims.quote: Several animal studies reported neutral or even beneficial effects of TMAO or its precursors in cardiovascular disease model systems, supporting the clinically proven beneficial effects of its precursor, L-carnitine, or a sea-food rich diet (naturally containing TMAO) on cardiometabolic health.

claims.claim: Single lean-vegan-donor fecal microbiota transplantation shifted gut microbiota composition toward a vegan profile but produced no functional change in TMAO production capacity or vascular inflammation parameters in metabolic syndrome patients.
claims.quote: With vegan-donor fecal microbiota transplantation, intestinal microbiota composition in metabolic syndrome patients, as monitored by global fecal microbial community structure, changed toward a vegan profile in some of the patients; however, no functional effects from vegan-donor fecal microbiota transplantation were seen on TMAO production, abdominal aortic 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake, or ex vivo cytokine production from peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
